ST.003Succession/Team/Decisions

He left to protect it: 143 days to walk away from the company he founded

He believed nothing would move without him — until he admitted that he was the one holding the company back.

Interview
Keisuke MoriRELAY Inc.　Founder
Interview & text
SECOND TAKE
Date
Sep 8, 2026
Read
7 min

In this story

  1. 01The bottleneck
  2. 02Before a successor
  3. 03The last day
  4. 04Outside

In briefThe decision in three lines

  1. Every decision ran through the founder, and the organization slowed down.
  2. Before choosing a successor, he gave up his own role.
  3. Over 143 days he handed over authority and stepped outside.

Every morning, Keisuke Mori’s desk was covered in notes asking him to decide something.

Nine years after founding the company, he believed making the calls was his responsibility — no one knew the business better. But that sense of responsibility was taking away his team’s chance to think.

From the board meeting where he proposed a new CEO to his last day in the office: 143 days. This isn’t a story about letting go of a company. It’s about prying himself loose from one.

Scene 01Admitting he was the bottleneck

What made you decide to step down?

MoriI took a week off, and every important decision stopped. Part of me was proud to be relied on that much. But I also thought: this isn’t an organization.

Couldn’t you have simply delegated?

MoriI tried, many times. But in the end I’d overrule people. What I hadn’t let go of wasn’t authority. It was being the person who knew the right answer.

Scene 02What he stopped before choosing a successor

Where did the handover start?

MoriWith speaking last in meetings. If I gave my opinion first, it became the answer. Then I wrote down everything only I knew about our history with each client.

Mori left more than a list of tasks. Failed proposals, days he broke a promise, the words that repaired a relationship — he wrote down the company’s memory.

MoriA clean manual isn’t enough to make decisions with. If you know where things went wrong, the next person is stronger for it.

Scene 03Setting the last day first

How did you arrive at 143 days?

MoriIf I waited for a perfect handover, I’d never leave. So I counted back from the day the new team could set the next business plan on their own.

Once the date was set, there were fewer requests for advice and more reports. People stopped bringing him questions for approval and started bringing their own decisions.

Scene 04The second take began outside the company

How do you feel about the company now?

MoriI miss it. But every time it moves forward on a decision I didn’t know about, I feel relieved. I thought the view I wanted most as a founder was one I could only see from the inside. It was the other way around.
